explanations.explanation: That's the one, friend. The prophet Isaiah says darkness covers the earth, "but the LORD will rise upon you, and His glory will appear over you." (Isaiah 60:2) Thick darkness over the peoples, and the LORD's glory over Zion. One little word, "but," and the whole mood flips.

I like the thinking, since I get a star in my sky for every finished cookie box. But Isaiah's verse doesn't mention a star. He says "…the LORD will rise upon you, and His glory will appear over you." (Isaiah 60:2) The light in this verse is the LORD's glory.

Locusts! Friend, that would be a whole different kind of chapter. The verse says darkness covers the earth, "but the LORD will rise upon you, and His glory will appear over you." (Isaiah 60:2) No bugs here, just glory over Zion.

It's the other way around, friend. Isaiah says, "Nations will come to your light, and kings to the brightness of your dawn." (Isaiah 60:3) The dark doesn't keep them away. They're headed toward the light. Kind of like how everybody ends up in my kitchen when the oven's warming up.

Right, they don't stay away. Isaiah says, "Nations will come to your light, and kings to the brightness of your dawn." (Isaiah 60:3) So the world is dark, and nations and even kings are coming to Zion's light. I'd show up for that too.

Yes, her own children. Isaiah says, "your sons will come from afar, and your daughters will be carried on the arm." (Isaiah 60:4) Sons coming from afar, daughters carried on the arm. Now that's a picture.

Prophets are a fun guess, but this verse doesn't mention them. Isaiah says, "your sons will come from afar, and your daughters will be carried on the arm." (Isaiah 60:4) The ones coming are Zion's sons and daughters.

Priests would make a good crowd, but the verse doesn't name them. It says, "your sons will come from afar, and your daughters will be carried on the arm." (Isaiah 60:4) Sons and daughters are the ones on the road.

Yes, the sea. Isaiah says Zion will be radiant and her heart will swell with joy, "…because the riches of the sea will be brought to you…" (Isaiah 60:5) And the wealth of the nations comes right along with it. That's a lot of arrivals for one city.

Deserts are a fair guess, friend, but this verse says something else. Isaiah says, "…the riches of the sea will be brought to you…" (Isaiah 60:5) The riches in this verse are the riches of the sea, along with the wealth of the nations.

Mountains are a solid guess, friend, but the verse goes another way. Isaiah says, "…the riches of the sea will be brought to you…" (Isaiah 60:5) The riches come from the sea, along with the wealth of the nations.

You got it, baker. Isaiah says, "…all from Sheba will come, bearing gold and frankincense and proclaiming the praises of the LORD." (Isaiah 60:6) Gold and frankincense, plus praise on the way in. I'd call that a gift with a soundtrack.

Those two sound like a great pair, but this verse doesn't list them. Isaiah says Sheba will come "…bearing gold and frankincense and proclaiming the praises of the LORD." (Isaiah 60:6) So the answer is gold and frankincense.

Fancy cloth would look nice, but it's not in this verse. Isaiah says Sheba will come "…bearing gold and frankincense and proclaiming the praises of the LORD." (Isaiah 60:6) That's gold and frankincense.
True! Isaiah says they come "…bearing gold and frankincense and proclaiming the praises of the LORD." (Isaiah 60:6) So they arrive with gifts and with praise. That's a whole lot of arriving, friend.

It's true, actually. Isaiah says they come "…bearing gold and frankincense and proclaiming the praises of the LORD." (Isaiah 60:6) They show up with gold and frankincense in their hands and the LORD's praises on their lips. Gifts AND praise, friend. Hard to top that.

That's it, the altar. The LORD says the rams of Nebaioth "…will serve you and go up on My altar with acceptance…" (Isaiah 60:7) Then He says He will adorn His glorious house. Nebaioth's rams are headed there.
Mountain is a fair guess, friend. But the LORD says the rams of Nebaioth "…will serve you and go up on My altar with acceptance…" (Isaiah 60:7) The word is altar.
A throne would sound grand, but it's not the word here. The LORD says the rams of Nebaioth "…will serve you and go up on My altar with acceptance…" (Isaiah 60:7) It's the altar.

Yes, the ships of Tarshish. The LORD says, "Surely the islands will wait for Me, with the ships of Tarshish in the lead, to bring your children from afar…" (Isaiah 60:9) They're in the lead. Front of the line, friend.

Chariots make a strong entrance, friend, but this verse is about the sea. The LORD says, "Surely the islands will wait for Me, with the ships of Tarshish in the lead, to bring your children from afar…" (Isaiah 60:9) Ships are leading this parade.

Horsemen would kick up some dust, but they aren't in this verse. The LORD says, "Surely the islands will wait for Me, with the ships of Tarshish in the lead, to bring your children from afar…" (Isaiah 60:9) The answer is the ships of Tarshish.

Not empty-handed, friend. The LORD says the ships will bring Zion's children from afar "…with their silver and gold, to the honor of the LORD your God, the Holy One of Israel, for He has glorified you." (Isaiah 60:9) They arrive with silver and gold, and it's all for the honor of the LORD.

Right, they bring plenty. The LORD says the ships will bring Zion's children from afar "…with their silver and gold, to the honor of the LORD your God, the Holy One of Israel, for He has glorified you." (Isaiah 60:9) Silver and gold ride along with them.

Mercy is the word. The LORD says, "Although I struck you in anger, yet in favor I will show you mercy." (Isaiah 60:10) That's a verse worth reading twice. The anger was real, and so is the favor and mercy that follows.
Wrath doesn't come after the favor here. The LORD says, "Although I struck you in anger, yet in favor I will show you mercy." (Isaiah 60:10) What He shows in favor is mercy.
Silence isn't what the LORD says here. He says, "Although I struck you in anger, yet in favor I will show you mercy." (Isaiah 60:10) What follows His favor is mercy.

Never, day or night. The LORD says, "Your gates will always stand open; they will never be shut, day or night…" (Isaiah 60:11) Open all day, open all night, and no sign hanging on the door. I'd leave my oven door open too, but that's a bad idea.

Closing at night sounds sensible, friend, but that's not what the verse says. The LORD says, "Your gates will always stand open; they will never be shut, day or night…" (Isaiah 60:11) Day and night are both covered.
That's a reasonable guess, but the verse doesn't make an exception. The LORD says, "Your gates will always stand open; they will never be shut, day or night…" (Isaiah 60:11) Always open, never shut.

True, and I think this one is heavy. The LORD says, "For the nation or kingdom that will not serve you will perish; it will be utterly destroyed." (Isaiah 60:12) It's a sober verse in a chapter full of light, and I'll just let it stand as written.

I think this one is heavy, friend, and the answer is true. The LORD says, "For the nation or kingdom that will not serve you will perish; it will be utterly destroyed." (Isaiah 60:12) That's what the verse says, plain and serious.

Sanctuary, yes. The LORD says Lebanon's cypress, elm and boxwood will come "…to adorn the place of My sanctuary, and I will glorify the place of My feet." (Isaiah 60:13) The trees are for His holy place. And the LORD Himself says He will glorify it.

A palace would be a showy spot for all that wood, but it's not the word here. The LORD says the trees will come "…to adorn the place of My sanctuary, and I will glorify the place of My feet." (Isaiah 60:13) The word is sanctuary.

Gardens would be a pretty spot for trees, friend, but the verse says something else. The LORD says they will come "…to adorn the place of My sanctuary, and I will glorify the place of My feet." (Isaiah 60:13) The word is sanctuary.
That's not how this verse goes, friend. Isaiah says, "The sons of your oppressors will come and bow down to you…" (Isaiah 60:14) They come to bow, not to attack. A very different kind of visit.

False, you've got it. Isaiah says, "The sons of your oppressors will come and bow down to you; all who reviled you will fall facedown at your feet…" (Isaiah 60:14) The sons of her oppressors come to bow down. And those who reviled her fall facedown at her feet.
Yes! They will "…call you the City of the LORD, Zion of the Holy One of Israel." (Isaiah 60:14) The people who once reviled Zion are the ones saying it. That's quite a turn.
Salt is a fun guess, friend, but it's not in the verse. Isaiah says they will "…call you the City of the LORD, Zion of the Holy One of Israel." (Isaiah 60:14) That's the name they use.
That's a nice name, but the verse has a different one. Isaiah says they will "…call you the City of the LORD, Zion of the Holy One of Israel." (Isaiah 60:14) The name is the City of the LORD.
Joy! The LORD says, "…I will make you an everlasting pride, a joy from age to age." (Isaiah 60:15) Forsaken and despised before, and now joy from age to age. That's a big change, friend.
Warning doesn't fit this verse, friend. The LORD says, "…I will make you an everlasting pride, a joy from age to age." (Isaiah 60:15) The word is joy.

A mystery would keep us guessing, but the verse is plain. The LORD says, "…I will make you an everlasting pride, a joy from age to age." (Isaiah 60:15) Zion has been forsaken and despised, and the LORD is the One who makes her an everlasting pride. The word that finishes it is joy.
True. The LORD says, "you will know that I, the LORD, am your Savior and your Redeemer, the Mighty One of Jacob." (Isaiah 60:16) Savior, Redeemer, Mighty One. Zion will know who He is.

I'd flip that one, friend. The LORD says, "you will know that I, the LORD, am your Savior and your Redeemer, the Mighty One of Jacob." (Isaiah 60:16) That makes the card true. Zion will know exactly who He is.

Silver! The LORD says, "Instead of bronze I will bring you gold; I will bring silver in place of iron, bronze instead of wood, and iron instead of stones." (Isaiah 60:17) Every swap in that list is a step up. I may need a swap like that for my own chef's hat.
Tin makes sense as a metal, but it's not in the list. The LORD says, "I will bring silver in place of iron, bronze instead of wood, and iron instead of stones." (Isaiah 60:17) The answer is silver.
Lead isn't in this one, friend. The LORD says, "I will bring silver in place of iron, bronze instead of wood, and iron instead of stones." (Isaiah 60:17) The swap for iron is silver.
True. The LORD says, "I will appoint peace as your governor and righteousness as your ruler." (Isaiah 60:17) Peace governing and righteousness ruling. That sounds like a great place to live.
This one is true, friend. The LORD says, "I will appoint peace as your governor and righteousness as your ruler." (Isaiah 60:17) Peace and righteousness are the ones in charge.
Salvation! The LORD says, "But you will name your walls Salvation and your gates Praise." (Isaiah 60:18) Walls named Salvation and gates named Praise. Now that's a sign worth hanging up.
Fortress sounds tough, friend, but it's not the name. The LORD says, "But you will name your walls Salvation and your gates Praise." (Isaiah 60:18) The walls are named Salvation.
A watchtower would be a handy thing on a wall, but it's not the name here. The LORD says, "But you will name your walls Salvation and your gates Praise." (Isaiah 60:18) The walls are named Salvation.
Yes, the LORD Himself. Isaiah says, "…the LORD will be your everlasting light, and your God will be your splendor." (Isaiah 60:19) The sun and moon are no longer her light, and the LORD is.
Lamps are a natural guess, friend, but they're not in this verse. Isaiah says, "…the LORD will be your everlasting light, and your God will be your splendor." (Isaiah 60:19) The light is the LORD.

Torches would light up a wall nicely, but they're not what the verse says. Isaiah says, "…the LORD will be your everlasting light, and your God will be your splendor." (Isaiah 60:19) The LORD Himself is the light.

True. Isaiah says, "…the LORD will be your everlasting light, and the days of your sorrow will cease." (Isaiah 60:20) Everlasting light, and sorrow comes to an end. That's a good line to hold onto, friend.
It's true, friend. Isaiah says, "…the LORD will be your everlasting light, and the days of your sorrow will cease." (Isaiah 60:20) The sorrow stops, and the light stays.

explanations.answer: So that He may be glorified
explanations.explanation: That's the reason the LORD gives. Zion's people are "…the branch of My planting, the work of My hands, so that I may be glorified." (Isaiah 60:21) The reason is the LORD's glory. Planted and made by Him, for Him.

explanations.answer: So that their name may be great
explanations.explanation: A great name sounds like a fine reason, but the LORD doesn't say that here. He calls them "…the branch of My planting, the work of My hands, so that I may be glorified." (Isaiah 60:21) The reason He gives is His own glory.

explanations.answer: So that they may rule the nations
explanations.explanation: Ruling the nations is a big guess, friend, but it's not what the verse says. The LORD calls them "…the branch of My planting, the work of My hands, so that I may be glorified." (Isaiah 60:21) The reason He gives is His glory.

In its time, and quickly. The LORD says, "I am the LORD; in its time I will accomplish it quickly." (Isaiah 60:22) The timing is in His hands, and when the time comes, He moves fast. That's a chapter finished, baker.
Slow is an understandable guess, friend, since waiting is a big part of Scripture. But the LORD says, "I am the LORD; in its time I will accomplish it quickly." (Isaiah 60:22) The word is quickly.

Walls do come up earlier in the chapter, but this verse doesn't set that as a condition. The LORD says, "I am the LORD; in its time I will accomplish it quickly." (Isaiah 60:22) It happens in its time, and quickly.
